MALL SECURITY

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With jingle bells playing in all the malls, tinsel sparkling all over, the festive shopping season is about to kick off – and thieves – are gearing up for the action too – we investigate new cri

Unique Selling Point:
- topical
- informative
- new crime trend
- advice to empower consumers / viewers

Summary:
We look at new crime trends, explore the psychology behind using children to commit petty crimes and ask what security measures are in place to safeguard consumers.

Further information:
SHOPPING CENTRE INDUSTRY IN NUMBERS:
There is around 25 million square meters of shopping space to let across over 2000 individual shopping centres in South Africa (2017 study conducted by MSCI on behalf of the South African Council of Shopping Centres).

FESTIVE SEASON SPIKE
With a marked increase in foot traffic and card swipes - the festive shopping season is normally associated with higher criminal activity, in particular attempted robberies at shopping malls and other petty crimes such as shoplifting and theft of and out of motor vehicles - The Crime Risk Initiative (CRI) of the Consumer Goods Council of South Africa (CGCSA)

CONSUMER SAFETY CONCERNS
At the 2014 Annual Congress of the South African Council of Shopping Centres, consumer retail property services company CBRE (leading global real estate services provider to the commercial, industrial, retail and investment markets )presented the results of a survey that identified South Africans’ top four concerns when choosing a mall to visit as:
- mall cleanliness,
- security,
- price of products,
- and availability of coffee shops and free Wi-Fi

Security is the second most significant concern for consumers!

NEW CRIME TRENDS
Petty crime is taking on a new face – adults are enlisting kids to the stealing. Criminologist Christiaan Bezuidenhoud explains that children are often dismissed and people are disarmed and less suspicious around them. With their guards down, unsuspecting consumers become the victims of petty crime – losing their cellphones, wallets and bags to kid crooks prompted by adults.

WHY CRIMINALS USE KIDS?
- When caught, the adults blame the children claiming innocence
- The charges kids would face are less severe than for adults
- They are usually not prosecuted

THE PSYCHOLOGY BEHIND IT
This type of coercion is a form of parental manipulation where the children are manipulated into doing things they would usually know are wrong by either a parent or adult known to them. There is also a level of conditioning involved. None of this is healthy behaviour, it is a form of abuse. We explore the psychological manipulation and impact this has on children that used in criminal activity.

MALL SECURITY CHALLENGES & INITIATIVES
Mall management teams and retailers spend millions every year analysing security risks and how they can be mitigated – but small time thieves are changing tactics and bringing in their secret weapons – seemingly innocent kids – to do the dirty work.

We speak to Fidelity Security who runs 85% of all mall security across the country about the trends, the counter measures and advice for consumers.

Script:


MALL SECURITY STRUCTURE

VO: With the festive season is in full swing, South Africans are gearing up for the holidays and giving in to the last minute shopping madness.

LINK: // Malls are bustling and retailers are raking in big bucks with flustered shoppers ticking off endless lists, making it a prime hunting ground for petty thieves with long fingers.
VO: Shoplifting, pickpocketing and general theft, rank amongst the most common crimes in the country, prevalent in areas with high-level economic activity.
With a marked increase in shopping mall foot traffic over December - Criminologist Professor Christiaan Bezuidenhout believes this type of shopping centre crime is bound to spike during the festive season.

CHRISTIAAN: shopping centres are a very nice enclosed space there’s people with their wallets, they want to come and shop - it’s a good opportunity for the motivated offender to strike. INT 1 M4

VO: But these thieves are changing tactics and bringing in a secret weapon to catch consumers and retailers off guard – they’re uisng, seemingly innocent children to do the dirty work.

CHRISTIAAN: You wouldn’t expect a child to steal from you // you don’t want to believe that they are little criminals INT 1 M17

VO: Shoppers agree, it a cunning approach.

VOX 3: it’s shocking it’s a disgrace
VOX 2: for the child it’s an abuse, it’s not acceptable at all
VOX 5: what have we come to as a country to be using children to commit crimes

SWANEPOEL: It is an unbelievable concept to grasp, however from a scientific point of view, not so strange, because you get the principle of criminalistic behaviour being carried over from generation to generation, // INT1 M2

VO: Children are often socialised and conditioned to see criminal acts as normal behaviour explains Clinical Psychologist Dr. Henk Swanepoel.

SWANEPOEL: //They see it as acceptable and from there on it becomes more a manifestation of behaviour as they get older into adulthood. INT1 M3

VO: Using children like this, makes it a near perfect crime according to Prof. Bezuidenhout.

CHRISTIAAN: // the adult can easily blame the child – say what have you done now? And sometimes they over discipline the child in front of the victim – I don’t know what went wrong, I don’t what’s wrong with my child, it’s a typical strategy. INT 1 M14

VO: With around 25 million square meters of shopping space across over 2000 individual shopping centres in South Africa , Fidelity Security covers a large percentage of the country’s malls – CEO Wahl Bartmann says using children to steal, is a daily phenomenon.

WAHL: Different children, parents, all together working together // as a syndicate – it’s become a type of business modus operandi that they use to secure and steal these goods, INT2 M4

VO: Professor Bezuidenhout explains it’s a well oiled operation with a network of people in on the job.

CHRISTIAAN: there’s the typical the look out, then the one that will, the so-called operator that will be with the children, that’s guarding the children, then you’ve got the children with specific roles, // in certain cases, children are sometimes to used as a decoy. //INT 1 M30

VO: This video surfaced at the end of November. Watch as this woman and three children loiter close to the table, where an unsuspecting woman is sitting with her handbag placed on the ground.

SWANEPOEL: // one can see she gradually moves closer and closer and then sad to say it seems that it’s habitual behaviour. She’s done this before.
DEVI: It looks very practiced.
SWANEPOEL: It does. INT1 M14

VO: Having snatched the bag without anyone noticing, the group casually walked off.

SWANEPOEL: It normalised the behaviour, it also shows them not to react in a panicky state. // and that they are actually used to doing that. It is a typical reaction from a psychological point of view in terms of anti-social behaviour where it is an act without remorse. INT1 M15

VO: Fidelity manages the security at this particular mall - further investigation revealed this wasn’t a once off case for the group.

WAHL: // that wasn’t the first bag that was stolen by that team – it happened before. // it is a team and picking up and going through all the video and facial recognition – we have picked up that they are involved with other instances as well.
DEVI: Using children
WAHL: Yes, using children 100% . INT 2 M10

VO: Globally, it’s a common trend – people are generally less suspicious of children and unwittingly are then more open to becoming victims.

LINK: There is nothing normal about this behavior. This is high-level psychological manipulation and conditioning at play here – it’s abuse.

SWANEPOEL: From developmental point of view the parent is seen as the authority figures, whatever is said or instructed by the parent is accepted by the child // so it’s not disputed by the child but the principle behind it is because the instruction comes from the parent that is why it is accepted. INT1 M6
DEVI: Some times it’s justified to children we need food, we are hungry yu need to do this for us…
SWANEPOEL: for a child that will make sense, they have to break the rules for something good, so the intention is good even though the behaviour is bad already there is a skewed perception of morality INT1 M24

VO: Besides manipulaton and socialisation, rewards are often used to get children to buy into the criminality notes Professor Bezuidenhout.

CHRISTIAAN: // sometimes they share the spoils from a crime with the child and that’s another way for the child to say wow! You know, there’s reinforcement and they will just and get involved with this because this is what the family do, // INT 1 M16 last third

SWANEPOEL: // their environment is teaching them to be deceitful and to be acceptant towards crimes and these crimes as they grow older escalate and they go over to more violent crime, substance abuse, etc. etc, it is a vicious cycle and then when they have children it continues. INT1 M19

VO: While this is first level crime, in the age of smartphones and gadget watches, pickpocketing can yield big returns.

CHRISTIAAN: If you’ve got a mobile phone of R15k and a tablet of R12k, a wallet full f cash, your cards, // it’s not nothing, and your car keys – sometimes they can even get away with your car at the end of the day – it’s not nothing – it’s serious. It’s a big difference between a loaf of bread because I’m hungry versus stealing a designer handbag of R5000 and all the contents of that hangbag – I mean that is a significant amount of money – that adds up. INT 1 M22

VO: According to Bartmann, thieving children are not limited to targeting consumers either.

WAHL: It’s not small quantities that are stolen, there’s a lot of shrinkage and you know items stolen from these stores INT 2 M1
DEVI: So we’re not just talking about petty crime, handbags, cellphone – you’re talking about children being used to steal goods from stores?
WAHL: It’s huge, and it’s been an Mo for a while now that they use their children as well where it’s not only the parents but also the children and everybody is involved in the crime. INT 2 M2

LINK: One of the draw cards for using children to commit criminal acts is that in South Africa, children under the age of 10 lack criminal capacity and are very rarely prosecuted.

CHRISTIAAN: // so that use these young children to commit the crime and leave the handbag or whatever item with the child so if they get caught // they responsibilise the child and blame the child, they don’t take the responsilbity. INT 1 M14

VO: But claiming ignorance of the alleged crime is not always going to cut it, every incident is taken seriously says Bartmann.

WAHL: We have a full process, we call the parents in, report it to shopping centre management as well as the SAPS. INT1 M10

CHRISTIAAN: //There is at least two charges against the mother // with the mother abusing the child // and obviously theft// and with the child it all depends on their criminal responsibility, their age, youthfulnees as it is known in the system, under 10 that child will be taken away// INT 1 M23

VO: While it’s classified as petty theft, combating this scourge is a priority for mall security. Teams have implemented intricate surveillance systems to keep shoppers safe from criminal elements.

WAHL: There is a lot of technology, CCTV systems, cameras, looking at profiling, looking at suspicious people, picking them up, using undercover staff in the areas to patrol the areas…. Monitor them, check them //. INT 2 M5

VO: But while shopping centre management teams and retailers beef up security in anticipation of festive crime spikes, consumers need to keep their wits about them too.

CHRISTIAAN: don’t focus too much on the modus operandi because they will change it according to the situation – they will adapt to their situation. // These children that have been socialised and conditioned by parents or adults will not blink an eye to steal from you // You are the victim – they want your stuff. INT 1 M30

VO: We explore the psychology driving this disturbing trend.


PROMO 3

CHRISTIAAN: // if they get caught they get // they responsibilise the child and blame the child, they don’t take the responsilbity. INT 1 M14


PROMO 4
VO: With jingle bells playing and tinsel sparkling all over malls, the festive shopping season has kicked off.

CHRISTIAAN: It’s a good opportunity for the motivated offender to strike. INT 1 M4

VO: Thieves are gearing up for the action with a new tactic using children to do the dirty work - taking advantage of their vulnerability and manipulating them into criminality.

SWANEPOEL: // so it’s not disputed by the child but the principle behind it is because the instruction comes from the parent that is why it is accepted. INT1 M6

VO: We investigate this new crime trend targeting consumers and retailers across South Africa.

metadata.Further information: SHOPPING CENTRE INDUSTRY IN NUMBERS: There is around 25 million square meters of shopping space to let across over 2000 individual shopping centres in South Africa (2017 study conducted by MSCI on behalf of the South African Council of Shopping Centres). FESTIVE SEASON SPIKE With a marked increase in foot traffic and card swipes - the festive shopping season is normally associated with higher criminal activity, in particular attempted robberies at shopping malls and other petty crimes such as shoplifting and theft of and out of motor vehicles - The Crime Risk Initiative (CRI) of the Consumer Goods Council of South Africa (CGCSA) CONSUMER SAFETY CONCERNS At the 2014 Annual Congress of the South African Council of Shopping Centres, consumer retail property services company CBRE (leading global real estate services provider to the commercial, industrial, retail and investment markets )presented the results of a survey that identified South Africans’ top four concerns when choosing a mall to visit as: - mall cleanliness, - security, - price of products, - and availability of coffee shops and free Wi-Fi Security is the second most significant concern for consumers! NEW CRIME TRENDS Petty crime is taking on a new face – adults are enlisting kids to the stealing. Criminologist Christiaan Bezuidenhoud explains that children are often dismissed and people are disarmed and less suspicious around them. With their guards down, unsuspecting consumers become the victims of petty crime – losing their cellphones, wallets and bags to kid crooks prompted by adults. WHY CRIMINALS USE KIDS? - When caught, the adults blame the children claiming innocence - The charges kids would face are less severe than for adults - They are usually not prosecuted THE PSYCHOLOGY BEHIND IT This type of coercion is a form of parental manipulation where the children are manipulated into doing things they would usually know are wrong by either a parent or adult known to them. There is also a level of conditioning involved. None of this is healthy behaviour, it is a form of abuse. We explore the psychological manipulation and impact this has on children that used in criminal activity. MALL SECURITY CHALLENGES & INITIATIVES Mall management teams and retailers spend millions every year analysing security risks and how they can be mitigated – but small time thieves are changing tactics and bringing in their secret weapons – seemingly innocent kids – to do the dirty work. We speak to Fidelity Security who runs 85% of all mall security across the country about the trends, the counter measures and advice for consumers.
